finding: §6.2.1 says the grade MUST be computed by cr and §6.2.2 rejects a false `probed` claim with exit 1, but nothing validates `cited`: the row requires only that the record references at least one concrete path:line outside the diff. cr never checks that the path exists, that the line exists at the current head, or that the referenced code bears on the summary. Any record can therefore be promoted from `argued` to `cited` (and so escape the §6.3 question forcing and become a posted assertion) by attaching an arbitrary path:line, at zero cost and leaving no trace. The asymmetry with §6.2.2 is the whole defect: the expensive grade is validated, the cheap one is not.
suggestion: Require cr to resolve every path:line in `evidence` against the current head and reject the record with exit 1 when it does not resolve, giving `cited` the §6.2.2 treatment already given to `probed`. Store the resolved content hash of each citation on the record, and state explicitly that cr cannot judge relevance, so a `cited` record MUST carry its citations verbatim into the draft block for the human to check.

finding: §6.3.3 grants --allow-argued-findings to override the argued-to-question forcing, and §6.3 carries no equivalent of §8.5.3 (there MUST be no configuration setting that removes the gate). Under §2.7 flags are layer 1 and CR_-prefixed environment variables are layer 2, so nothing in the spec stops CR_ALLOW_ARGUED_FINDINGS=1 in a shell profile from disabling the forcing permanently and invisibly for every round. Recording the use in the round summary (§6.3.2, §6.3.3) is post-hoc bookkeeping that nobody reads before the comment reaches the author. This is the documented escape from the one rule the tool exists to enforce.
suggestion: Delete §6.3.3, or narrow it to a single named record id with a mandatory reason string, forbid it from the environment and config layers with a clause mirroring §8.5.3, and require an overridden record to render a visible marker in its draft block so the human triaging sees exactly which records skipped the forcing.

finding: §6.3.1 forces an `argued` record to `kind: question` only 'at record time'. §7.2 then lets the user edit marker fields, lists only the finding-to-question direction as a triage verb, and §7.2.1-2 validate a marker only for malformedness and anchor resolution. §8 never re-checks grade against kind before posting. A draft whose marker is edited from `kind=question` back to `kind=finding` on an `argued` record therefore has no specified behaviour, so no pass/fail test can be written for the rule that an argued record is never posted as an assertion — the one rule the spec says must be enforced in `cr` rather than in the prompt.
suggestion: Add to §7.2: `cr post` MUST re-apply §6.3 to every block before posting, and MUST reject with exit code 1, naming the record id, any block whose record is graded `argued` and whose marker says `kind=finding`, unless `--allow-argued-findings` is passed and recorded per §6.3.3. State that promoting a question to a finding is not a supported triage verb.

finding: §8.5 makes --confirm the entire human gate, but per §2.1 the agent is the process that runs every cr command, so `cr draft && cr post --confirm` posts every block exactly as rendered. Nothing in §7.1, §7.2 or §8.5 requires any evidence that a human opened, read, or touched rounds/<n>/draft.md: no mtime comparison, no TTY requirement, no explicit acceptance step. The §7.2 table makes this worse by defining the no-action row (leaves a block unchanged) as post-as-rendered, so the failure mode of an absent human is that everything ships. P4 and VISION §2.4 rest entirely on the social convention that a person types the flag, which is not a mechanism.
suggestion: Require `cr post --confirm` to prove the draft was seen: record the content hash and mtime of draft.md at render time and refuse to post when neither changed, or add an explicit `cr draft --accept` step that stamps meta.json with an acceptance token that `cr post` demands. Refuse --confirm when stdin is not a TTY unless an explicit `--approved-by <name>` is supplied and recorded in the round.

finding: Convergence condition 4 lists the blocking states as `draft, queued, posted, awaiting-author, answered, verifying, stale-anchor` and omits `regressed`. §9.1.2 declares only `fixed` and `accepted` terminal, so a `regressed` record of severity `critical` — created by §9.4.3 precisely because a fix broke something — does not block convergence and the PR is reported as converged. Condition 3 has a second gap: `has an open unimplemented-claim record` uses `open`, a word the §9.1 state enum never defines.
suggestion: Add `regressed` to the blocking list in §10.2.4, and define `open` in §10.2.3 as any state other than `fixed`, `accepted` and `discarded` (or enumerate it), so both conditions are computable from the state field alone.

finding: §4.5.4 says cr MUST NOT report a review as complete without stating which axes did not run, but the four convergence conditions of §10.2 say nothing about axis availability. A PR with no resolvable issue key (§3.2 marks the intent axis unavailable) and a profile with no test command (§4.5.2 disables the test axis) satisfies all four conditions on two axes and prints converged — the strongest completeness claim cr makes — while half the review never happened. §10.1.3 reports the axes elsewhere in the same command's output, which is not the same as qualifying the verdict itself.
suggestion: Require the verdict to carry its own caveat: `cr status` MUST print the convergence verdict together with the axes that did not run and their reasons, and MUST render it as converged on N of 4 axes whenever any axis was disabled or unavailable. Never emit an unqualified converged, in text or in JSON.

finding: §6.1 makes record ids `f<n>` 'stable for the life of the PR', i.e. PR-scoped, but the §11 table gives `cr resolve <id> --confirm` and `cr answer <question-id> <text>` no PR or repository argument, so `f3` names a different record in every PR and the command is unresolvable. `cr stats`, `cr waivers list|remove`, and `cr rules suggest` likewise take no repository argument while waivers are stored per repository (§2.2, §7.4.1) and harvesting scans 'comments posted from recorded rounds' (§2.6.3.1) with no stated scope. Tests for these commands have no way to construct an unambiguous invocation.
suggestion: Either make record ids globally unique by prefixing owner/repo/pr, or add a `<pr>` argument to `resolve` and `answer`. Add an explicit repository scope to `stats`, `waivers`, and `rules suggest`, and state the default when the command is run inside a git repository (§11.1 already defines `--repo`).

finding: --quiet is specified only as suppress informational messages, with no carve-out, while §5.6.4 (the probe cap being hit MUST be reported, never silently applied), §4.5.4 (disabled and unavailable axes), §6.3.2 (the forcing count per class), §5.6.3 (the local test-run collision warning) and §8.1.4 (the missing-question warning) are all informational messages whose entire purpose is honesty. Under §2.7 a CR_QUIET environment variable set once in a shell profile mutes them permanently. This is a configuration setting that weakens exactly the guarantees §8.5.3 protects for the confirmation gate alone.
suggestion: Define a class of mandatory disclosures — axis availability and reasons, argued-forcing counts, probe cap hits, waiver and dedup counts, and every validation warning — and state that --quiet, --compact and any CR_ variable MUST NOT suppress them. Route them to stderr and include them in the JSON output regardless of verbosity flags.

finding: The state layout table defines no location for three kinds of state that later sections require. §2.6.1 mandates rules resolving per-repository, then global, then profile built-in, but §2.2 lists paths for roles at both layers and none for rules. §7.3.1 requires every triage event to be recorded and §7.3.3 needs at least `stats.min_samples` (8) events per class to fire a demotion candidate, yet §11 gives `cr stats` no `<pr>` argument and §2.3's per-PR table has no triage-event file — so the statistics have no store, and no defined scope (per-PR, per-repo, or global). §10.3 requires a per-round summary with no file to hold it.
suggestion: Add `~/.cr/rules/<id>.json` and `~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/rules/<id>.json` to the §2.2 table; add a repository-scoped `~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/triage.ndjson` (repo scope, so `stats.min_samples` is reachable, and matching the repo scope §7.4.1 already gives waivers); add `rounds/<n>/summary.json` to the §2.3 table. State in §7.3 which scope `cr stats` aggregates over.

finding: Later sections mandate durable data with no file in §2.2 or §2.3 to hold it: triage events with class, axis, role, grade and action (§7.3.1); dismissed rule hits counted per rule (§2.6.1.6); per-rule hit and record history across the last `rules.dead_after` rounds, which spans PRs (§2.6.3.4); round summary counts (§10.3); and state transitions with timestamp, head SHA and actor (§9.1.1). §7.3 `cr stats`, §2.6.3.1 `cr rules suggest` and `cr rules list --dead` all read across PRs and rounds, yet take no repository or PR argument in §11 and no cross-PR index exists. As written these commands have nothing to read.
suggestion: Extend §2.2 and §2.3 with the missing stores and their scope: `~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/triage.ndjson`, `.../rule-stats.ndjson`, `.../rounds.ndjson` for the cross-PR history, plus per-PR `transitions.ndjson` and `rounds/<n>/summary.json`. State that `cr stats`, `cr rules suggest` and `cr rules list --dead` are repository-scoped and resolve the repository from `--repo` or from the working directory.

finding: §2.6.1.1 evaluates a `detect` block 'over the changed lines of the diff only'. It is not stated whether removed (LEFT) lines count as changed — under which a rule banning a symbol fires on the very line that removed it, producing exactly the wrong assertion this project is built to avoid — nor whether context lines count, nor whether the regex is applied per line or over the concatenated changed region (which decides whether a multi-line pattern can ever match), nor whether the diff marker character is part of the matched text.
suggestion: Restrict detection to added lines on the RIGHT side, state that the pattern is applied to each added line individually with the leading diff marker stripped, and state that multi-line patterns are out of scope in v0.1 alongside the `detect.mode = regex` restriction.

finding: §2.6.1.1 restricts mechanical detection to `the changed lines of the diff only`, and §2.6.1.3 says a hit MUST grade the record `cited`. But §6.2 defines `cited` as `References at least one concrete path:line outside the diff`, and §6.2.1 says the grade MUST be computed by cr from the record. A rule hit's only citation is inside the diff, so cr computes `argued`, and §6.3.1 then forces it to `kind: question`. Two MUSTs cannot both hold: the same record is required to be `cited` and computed as `argued`.
suggestion: Redefine `cited` in §6.2 as `references at least one concrete path:line that is not the finding's own anchor` (or add an explicit third clause: `or carries a rule id whose detector matched a concrete location`). State which clause a rule hit satisfies, so the grade function has one deterministic answer.

finding: §2.6.1.3 grades a regex hit `cited` on the ground that the rule plus the matched location is the citation, but §2.6.1.1 restricts detection to the changed lines of the diff while §6.2 defines `cited` as a path:line outside the diff. The two grading rules contradict each other and §6.2.1 names cr as the single computer of the grade with no tie-break. Worse, §2.6.1.5 states that detection reports hits and never verdicts, yet the grade it hands out is precisely the one that licenses assertion under §6.3. A newly written, imprecise pattern therefore asserts at colleagues until §2.6.1.6 has accumulated enough dismissals for anyone to notice.
suggestion: Either extend §6.2 to admit a rule id plus a matched in-diff location as a fourth citation form explicitly, or grade rule hits `argued` until the agent confirms them. In both cases make a rule's grade depend on its own dismissal record: a rule with fewer than `stats.min_samples` observations, or above `stats.demote_threshold`, produces questions rather than findings.

finding: §2.6.2.1 generates a code suggestion by regex replacement, and §2.6.2.2 sends it through §8.2 — which validates only placement: a contiguous range, within one hunk, with leading whitespace preserved. Nothing checks that the replacement parses, compiles, or preserves behaviour. On GitHub a suggestion block is one click from a commit on the author's branch, so this is the highest-cost wrong assertion in the whole spec: not a wrong sentence but a wrong commit, made by the author in good faith on cr's authority. The sandbox of §5.1 already exists at the PR head and is never used for this.
suggestion: Require every mechanically generated (non-agent-authored) suggestion to be applied in the sandbox and verified before it may be drafted — at minimum that the file still parses, and where a test filter is available that the §5.2.2 baseline does not regress. Drop the suggestion and keep the record when verification fails, exactly as §2.6.2.2 already prescribes for placement failures, and count sandbox-verified suggestions in §10.1.

finding: §3.3 defines `hash` as a 'Content hash used to detect issue drift' and §3.3.3 requires `cr` to 'report which claim hashes no longer match' while forbidding silent re-extraction. If the hash covers the stored claim text it always matches itself; identifying which individual claims drifted requires re-deriving claims from the new issue text, which the same section makes the agent's job and which §2.1 forbids `cr` from judging. There is no observable input against which a stored claim hash can fail to match, so no pass/fail test exists for §3.3.3.
suggestion: Specify that `cr` stores a hash of the whole fetched issue text and reports only that the issue text changed, with a textual diff, then requires the agent to re-record claims; or define `hash` as the hash of a verbatim source span recorded on the claim, so `cr` can mechanically re-check each span against the new issue text.

finding: §3.4.3 clusters by 'same file and same enclosing symbol when detectable; otherwise same file and adjacency within `cluster.gap_lines`'. Neither term is pinned. Nothing says how `cr` detects an enclosing symbol (the only related config is `symbols.lang`, described as a 'hint'), what happens when detection succeeds for one hunk and fails for its neighbour, or how adjacency is measured — end line of hunk A to start line of hunk B, in old-file or new-file coordinates, counting context lines or only changed lines. §2.1.1 nevertheless requires the same inputs to produce the same units, so unit ids are contract, not incidental output.
suggestion: State the symbol-detection mechanism (and that a profile lacking it always falls through to the adjacency rule), define adjacency as 'first changed line of the later hunk minus last changed line of the earlier hunk, in new-file coordinates, excluding context lines', and add a worked example at the default gap_lines of 12.

finding: §3.4.3 ends with 'otherwise one unit per hunk', while §3.4.4 requires that 'A unit MUST NOT exceed `cluster.max_lines` changed lines (default 80); a larger cluster MUST be split.' A single hunk with more than 80 changed lines satisfies neither: it is already one unit per hunk and no stated rule can split it. No splitting algorithm is given at all — at line boundaries, at symbol boundaries, evenly, or greedily — so neither unit count nor unit ids are reproducible for any diff containing a large hunk, which is the common case in a rename or a generated-file edit.
suggestion: Say explicitly what happens to an oversized single hunk: either allow it as one unit carrying an `oversized` flag that is reported, or specify a deterministic split (e.g. consecutive slices of at most max_lines changed lines in new-file order). State how split units are numbered so ids stay stable across rounds.

finding: §3.5.3 requires a finding to be suppressed when its `anchor and class match an existing human thread`. Existing human threads are free prose written by another reviewer and carry no class; assigning one requires reading the comment and judging what defect it names, which §2.1 forbids cr from doing and §1.3.4 forbids outright. As stated the match is not computable by a deterministic tool.
suggestion: Move the semantic half to the agent: cr attaches every ingested thread whose anchor is within N lines of a candidate finding to that finding's unit brief and marks the finding `suppression-candidate`; the agent decides and calls a command to suppress with a recorded reason. Alternatively keep the mechanical rule but base it on anchor overlap alone, and say so.

finding: §3.5.3 suppresses a finding 'whose anchor and class match an existing human thread'. But §3.5.1 ingests threads with 'author, body, anchor, resolution state, and replies' — no class is ever assigned to an ingested thread, and nothing defines how a GitHub thread's path and line compare against the anchor object of §9.2 (exact line equality, same hunk, or within the context window). The resulting marker `suppressed_by_thread` also appears in no §9.1 state row. The QA checklist expects 'a finding matching an existing human thread is suppressed' to be testable; as written the key has an undefined component and an undefined comparison.
suggestion: Define how a class is derived for an ingested thread, or drop class from the key and match on anchor proximity alone with a stated rule (e.g. same path and the finding line within N lines of the thread line). Add `suppressed_by_thread` to the §9.1 table, or state that it is a suppression reason stored on the record rather than a state.

finding: §4.1.3 requires an unimplemented-claim item for every claim mapped to zero units — a record with no corresponding code location by construction. But §6.1.2 requires every finding to 'carry an anchor that resolves to a line in the current head', §7.1.1 requires every draft marker to carry `path` and `line`, and §8.3 posts everything as a single GitHub review whose comments are anchored to a file and line. The spec never says where an unimplemented-claim record is anchored or how it is posted, so its draft rendering, its §8.2 validation, and its posting path are all untestable.
suggestion: Introduce a record-level location kind: allow `anchor: null` for claim-level records, require them to be rendered in the review body rather than as line comments, and exempt them from §6.1.2 and §7.1.1's path/line requirement. Update §8.3 to state that the review body carries the unanchored records.

finding: §4.1.5 says that if the context store `already explains an unmapped unit`, the item MUST NOT be raised and the explaining note MUST be cited in the coverage cell. Deciding whether a free-text note explains a block of changed code is a semantic judgement, and §2.1 states that cr `never decides whether code is correct` while §2.5 reserves judgement for roles. The requirement has no actor and cannot be met mechanically.
suggestion: Name the actor: cr loads all notes for the issue key into the unit brief and marks the unmapped-unit item as `suppressible-by-note`; the agent records the suppression together with the note id, and cr validates that a cited note exists. Apply the same actor-naming pass to §4.4.1 and §4.4.2.

finding: §4.1.5: 'If the context store already explains an unmapped unit, the item MUST NOT be raised and the explaining note MUST be cited in the coverage cell.' No actor is named and no matching criterion is given. `cr` cannot decide whether a prose note 'explains' a unit without forming a judgement, which §2.1 forbids; if the agent decides, the requirement should be phrased as an agent obligation with a recorded link. The project QA checklist treats this as a deterministic behaviour ('a recorded note suppresses the matching unmapped-unit question'), so a tester has a required behaviour with no decidable input.
suggestion: Make the linkage explicit and mechanical: the agent records `explained_by: <note-id>` on the unit through a command, and `cr` suppresses the item only when that field is present, citing the referenced note in the cell. §4.1.5 then has a deterministic pass/fail and no judgement lands in `cr`.

finding: §4.3.1 requires `cr` to 'search the repository for candidate pre-existing symbols' for every function, method, or class added by the diff, and §4.3.2 to rank candidates 'using name similarity and signature shape'. No similarity metric, no acceptance threshold, no cap on candidates per symbol, and no search mechanism are specified; `symbols.lang` is only a 'hint'. Since this is `cr`'s work and §2.1.1 requires reproducibility, the candidate list is part of the contract, yet no assertion can be written about it.
suggestion: Pin the mechanism: name the similarity function (e.g. normalised edit distance over identifiers split on case and underscore), the minimum score for a candidate, the maximum number of candidates attached per new symbol, the per-profile search command, and the deterministic tie ordering.

finding: §4.3.1 requires cr to find `every function, method, or class added by the diff` and search the whole repository for candidate pre-existing symbols, and §4.3.2 requires ranking by `name similarity and signature shape`. No mechanism, index, similarity metric, threshold, or candidate cap is specified; the only related config is `symbols.lang`, described in §2.4 merely as a `Language hint`. §14.1 caps runtime dependencies at git, gh and the tracker command, so no external indexer may be invoked. §3.4.3 leans on the same undefined capability with `same enclosing symbol when detectable` and never says what makes a symbol detectable. This is the largest block of behaviour an implementer would have to invent outright, and its output feeds a review axis.
suggestion: Pin the mechanism: name the extraction method per language (for example a declaration regex set carried on the profile, or an embedded parser), define `signature shape` concretely (arity plus parameter and return type tokens), define the similarity function and the score threshold, cap candidates per unit, and specify the required behaviour when `symbols.lang` is absent or unsupported — most likely disabling the reinvention part of the convention axis and reporting it as unavailable per §4.5.4. Do the same for `detectable` in §3.4.3, or make symbol-based clustering explicitly optional with adjacency as the declared fallback.

finding: §2.2 states cr `MUST NOT write inside the repository under review`, yet §5.1.1 requires creating a git worktree, which writes registration metadata into that repository's `.git/worktrees/<name>` — §5.1.5's `remove the worktree and its registration` concedes the registration exists. Separately, nothing specifies how the PR head becomes available locally: for a fork PR or an unfetched branch, `git worktree add <sha>` fails because the object is absent, and §2.1.2 only permits network writes, leaving the required fetch unstated.
suggestion: Add an explicit carve-out to §2.2: cr may create and remove its own git worktree registration under `.git/worktrees/`, and MUST NOT touch tracked files, the index, HEAD, or any other ref. Add a numbered item to §5.1 requiring cr to fetch the PR head ref (including the `refs/pull/<n>/head` case for forks) before creating the worktree, and to fail with exit 3 naming the fetch command when it cannot.

finding: §5.1.6 recreates a sandbox only when 'its head no longer matches the PR head'. §5.3.3 requires a mutation to be reverted 'even when the run fails or times out' but is silent about `cr` being killed mid-probe and about a revert that itself fails. A sandbox left with an applied mutation still has the matching head, so no stated condition detects it, and the next baseline run of §5.2.2 or probe of §5.3 silently reports results produced from mutated code — a probed grade resting on a corrupted experiment. Nothing in the spec lets a test assert recovery.
suggestion: Require `cr` to verify the sandbox worktree is clean (no modified or untracked files outside the declared `sandbox.copy` paths) before every test and probe run, and to recreate it or fail with exit code 4 otherwise. Require the revert to be verified after the run and the probe recorded as `error` when verification fails.

finding: Mutation-probe results are interpreted as raw runner outcomes with no cross-check, so the strongest evidence grade can be awarded vacuously. §5.3.4 grades a finding `probed` on `no-test-failed`, but a `--filter` that matches zero tests produces exactly that outcome — an assertion posted with maximum authority backed by an experiment that executed nothing. Symmetrically, §5.3.5 treats `failed` as disproof, but §5.2.2 exists precisely because the suite may already be red at that filter; §5.3 never references the baseline, so a pre-existing failure silently suppresses a real gap. §5.5's probe record has no field for how many tests ran, so neither check is even expressible against stored state.
suggestion: Add `tests_run` (and ideally `tests_failed`) to the §5.5 probe record, and add to §5.3: a probe whose `tests_run` is zero MUST be recorded with result `error` and MUST NOT grade any finding; and a `no-test-failed` or `failed` result MUST be compared against the same-head baseline run of §5.2.2, with a result that merely reproduces a baseline failure recorded as `inconclusive` rather than as disproof.

finding: §5.3.4 states that a no-test-failed result proves the gap and grades the finding `probed` — the only grade licensed to assert without qualification. But the filter in §5.3.2 is agent-supplied and nothing constrains it: a filter narrow enough to select tests unrelated to the mutated file guarantees no-test-failed. §5.2.2 requires an unfiltered baseline so pre-existing failures are never misattributed, but there is no symmetric protection against a filter too narrow to see the mutation. The strongest evidence cr can produce is manufacturable with one argument, and unlike §6.2.2 nothing rejects it.
suggestion: Require a no-test-failed result to be confirmed by an unfiltered or profile-default-scope re-run before it may grade a finding `probed`, or require cr to record which test files the filter actually selected and to refuse the `probed` grade when none of them exercise the mutated path. Carry the filter verbatim into the drafted evidence so the author can check the scope of the experiment.

finding: The `result` enum `no-test-failed, failed, passed, error, timeout` is shared by both probe kinds and its meaning inverts between them. §5.3.4 makes `no-test-failed` prove a mutation gap and §5.3.5 makes `failed` disprove it, while §5.4.3 says `A failing gap probe means the behaviour is wrong` and §5.4.4 says `A passing gap probe means only the test is missing` — the opposite polarity, with no statement of which enum values `failing` and `passing` map to. `no-test-failed` and `passed` are also indistinguishable for a suite that exits 0. Nothing states which gap-probe result grades a finding `probed`, so §6.2's `a result that supports the claim` is undecidable for kind `gap`.
suggestion: Add a table mapping (kind, runner exit outcome) to a `result` value and to the grade it licenses: mutation + suite green => `no-test-failed` => probed; mutation + suite red => `failed` => finding MUST NOT be raised; gap + new test red => `failed` => probed, severity >= high; gap + new test green => `passed` => probed, severity <= medium. Drop whichever of `passed`/`no-test-failed` becomes redundant, or scope each value to one kind.

finding: No schema table in the spec (§2.4, §2.5, §2.6, §3.3, §5.5, §6.1) marks fields required or optional, yet §6.5.2 makes `cr merge` fail with exit 1 on 'Missing required fields', §2.5.3 aborts on a 'malformed' role or profile with exit 3, and §2.6.5 does the same for a rule. Several §6.1 fields are plainly conditional (`rule`, `claim`, `probe`, `suggestion`, `thread_id`), and 'malformed' is never defined — invalid JSON, missing field, unknown field, or out-of-enum value. The validation test suite that gates three exit codes cannot be written.
suggestion: Add a required/optional column to every schema table, mark conditionally-required fields with their condition (e.g. `probe` required when `grade = probed`), and define 'malformed' as: not valid JSON, a missing required field, or a value outside a declared enum. State whether unknown fields are rejected or ignored.

finding: The 18-field record schema has no field for four relationships other sections mandate. §3.5.3 requires a finding suppressed by an existing human thread to be "recorded as `suppressed_by_thread`" — that is neither a §6.1 field nor a §9.1 state. §6.4.3 requires suppressed duplicates to be "retained with a pointer to the representative" — no pointer field exists. §9.4.3 requires a regressed record's replacement to be "linked to the original" — no link field exists. §10.1.5 requires reporting "probes that changed a finding's grade", which needs grade history; `grade` is a single scalar and §5.5.1 makes probe records immutable, so the change is unrecoverable.
suggestion: Add the missing fields to the §6.1 table: `duplicate_of` (representative record id), `supersedes`/`superseded_by` (regression link), `suppressed_by` (thread id, with the reason enumerated alongside §9.1's states), and either a `grade_history` array or a `grade_source` field recording what last set the grade.

finding: §6.2.1 requires the grade to be 'computed by `cr` from the record, never asserted by the agent', and `cited` turns on a 'concrete `path:line` outside the diff'. The only field that can carry a citation is `evidence`, described in §6.1 as free prose ('What supports it, including cited `path:line`'). No citation format is pinned, nor whether the path must exist at the current head, nor whether the line must exist, nor whether 'outside the diff' means a file absent from the diff or a line outside any changed hunk of a changed file. Grade computation — and therefore §6.3's forcing — is not deterministically testable.
suggestion: Add a structured `citations` array of `{path, line}` to §6.1 and compute the grade from that field alone. Define 'outside the diff' as 'the (path, line) pair falls in no hunk of the current diff', and require `cr` to verify each cited path and line resolves at the current head, rejecting the record with exit 1 otherwise.

finding: Grade computation is defined in three places with mutually incompatible rules. §6.2 defines `cited` as "References at least one concrete `path:line` outside the diff" and §6.2.1 says the grade MUST be computed by cr from the record. But §2.6.1.3 says a mechanical rule hit MUST be graded `cited`, and §2.6.1.1 restricts detection to the changed lines of the diff only — so a rule hit can never satisfy §6.2's own definition of `cited`. Separately §4.4.4 says a test-adequacy finding without a probe MUST be graded `argued`, which overrides §6.2 for one axis: such a finding may well cite an existing test file outside the diff and would compute to `cited` under §6.2. An implementer cannot write a single grade function that satisfies all three.
suggestion: Make §6.2 the single normative definition and express the other two as inputs to it. Either widen `cited` to "references at least one concrete `path:line`, which for a rule hit is the matched location and for reinvention is the candidate symbol", or add an explicit fourth input to the grade function (`rule_hit`). For §4.4.4, restate it as "a test-adequacy finding may not cite the absence of a test as evidence" so the outcome falls out of §6.2 rather than contradicting it.

finding: §6.2 defines `cited` as 'References at least one concrete `path:line` outside the diff'. §2.6.1.3 requires a mechanical rule hit to be graded `cited` 'because the rule together with the matched location is the citation', but §2.6.1.1 restricts detection to 'the changed lines of the diff only' — so the only location a rule hit can cite is inside the diff. A test asserting that a rule hit grades `cited` and a test asserting that `cited` requires an out-of-diff citation cannot both pass.
suggestion: Either drop 'outside the diff' from §6.2 and define `cited` as 'references at least one resolvable `path:line`, or a rule id together with its matched location', or add rule hits as an explicit third qualifying source in the §6.2 table row.

finding: §6.3.3 introduces `--allow-argued-findings`, which lets any caller post an `argued` record as an assertion. This contradicts §6.3.1's forcing and the project invariant that the forcing happens in cr "so no agent can talk its way past it" — a command-line flag is precisely the surface an agent controls. The flag is also absent from §11's command surface and §11.1's global-flag table, so its scope ("a single command" — which commands?) is undefined, and §8.5.3's "no configuration setting removes the gate" has no counterpart forbidding a flag that removes this gate.
suggestion: Either delete §6.3.3, or restrict it so the escape hatch is not agent-reachable: require it on `cr post` only, alongside `--confirm`, so a human is already in the loop, and state in §6.3 that it MUST NOT be accepted by `cr record` or `cr merge`. Whichever is chosen, add the flag to §11.1 and add a sentence naming which commands honour it.

finding: §7.2 says triage happens by editing the file and that `cr post` interprets the result, so a deleted block only becomes a discard and a waiver when post runs. §7.1.5 requires the draft to be regenerable and to preserve `existing bodies for records the user already edited`. Two problems follow. First, cr has no stored copy of what it originally rendered — §2.3 keeps only `draft.md` and `posted.json` — so `already edited` is not detectable. Second, regenerating before posting reinstates every deleted block, silently reversing a discard, which contradicts the promise that a deleted finding never returns.
suggestion: Persist the rendered body per record (for example `rounds/<n>/rendered.json`) so an edit is detected by comparison, and specify that `cr draft` itself reads the existing `draft.md` first and records deletions as discards plus waivers before re-rendering, so regeneration never resurrects a deleted block. State the required behaviour when a record was deleted and its waiver already exists.

finding: §7.2 states that `cr post` interprets the edited draft, so a deleted block becomes a discard plus a waiver only at post time. §7.1.5 makes the draft regenerable and requires preserving bodies for records the user already edited — but a deleted block has no body to preserve, so any `cr draft` run between the human's deletion and `cr post` re-renders the deleted record and it posts. A reviewer who deletes a false positive and then re-runs `cr draft` after recording a probe or answering a question silently loses the discard, and the item they rejected reaches the author.
suggestion: Make deletion durable at detection rather than at post time: have `cr draft` diff the on-disk draft against the version it last rendered, record deletions as discards and waivers immediately, and refuse to regenerate over a modified draft without a --force that names what will be lost. State explicitly that a regenerated draft MUST NOT re-render a record discarded in an earlier edit of the same round.

finding: §7.4.1 keys a waiver on (class, anchor content hash, normalised summary). Two of the three components are volatile. The summary is agent-composed English that the next round's agent will word differently, and the anchor content hash changes whenever the author edits the anchored lines — which is exactly what happens between rounds and exactly when the waiver is needed. The waiver therefore misses in precisely the case it exists for, and a discarded false positive is re-raised at the same colleague. This contradicts VISION §2.5 (deleted findings never come back) and the §7.2 promise that deletion is the discard verb.
suggestion: Key the waiver on stable components only — (class, path, rule id when present) plus a coarse locality such as the enclosing symbol name or the migrated anchor identity of §9.2 rather than a raw content hash — and keep the summary as recorded metadata outside the key. If a similarity component is retained, define its normalisation and require near-miss waivers to be surfaced in the draft (this resembles waiver w3) rather than silently re-raised.

finding: §6.3.1 forces `kind: question`, but the reader never sees `kind` — they see the agent-composed body, and §8.1.2 says cr MUST NOT compose or translate it. §8.1.4 only requires cr to warn when a kind=question body contains no explicit question, and a warning does not block posting; §11.1 --quiet suppresses informational messages outright. A forced question can therefore be posted with a body phrased as a flat assertion, which means the argued-to-question mechanism (P2, P3, VISION §2.3) is metadata that is never enforced at the only point where trust is actually spent.
suggestion: Make the check blocking rather than advisory: a kind=question body in which cr cannot detect a question MUST fail with exit code 1 naming the record id. Specify the detection precisely and language-independently, since cr forms no opinion and calls no model — for example require at least one question mark, or have `cr draft` pre-render a required interrogative closing line that the human may edit but not delete.

finding: §8.3.1 requires all comments in a round to be posted `as one GitHub review`. The GitHub review-creation call is atomic: if any comment position is invalid the whole request is rejected and no review or thread is created. §8.4.2's `If individual comments are rejected by GitHub, the successful ones MUST be recorded` therefore describes a partial-success mode that cannot occur while §8.3.1 holds, and the only way to produce it is to fall back to posting comments individually — which breaks the single-notification guarantee that §8.3.1 exists to provide.
suggestion: State which MUST wins. Either declare the post all-or-nothing (a rejected comment fails the whole review, exit 4, nothing marked posted, and the offending record ids reported) and delete §8.4.2's partial-success clause, or specify an explicit two-attempt protocol: on rejection, report the offending records, drop them, and re-issue a single review with the remainder only after the user re-confirms.

finding: §8.4.1 and §8.4.2 describe incompatible outcomes for the same failure, and both sit under §8.3.1's requirement that all comments be posted as one GitHub review. If there is one review call, its failure is all-or-nothing and §8.4.1 applies; there is no state in which "individual comments are rejected" while "the successful ones" exist. Reaching §8.4.2's behaviour requires falling back to per-comment posting, which breaks §8.3.1's single-notification guarantee — the stated reason for batching. As written the implementer must choose one section to violate.
suggestion: Decide the model explicitly. Recommended: keep §8.3.1 absolute, drop §8.4.2's partial-success case, and replace it with a pre-flight validation requirement — every comment's anchor and suggestion is validated locally before the single call, so a rejection is a bug rather than an expected path — and specify that a rejected review leaves all records unposted with exit code 4 and the rejected comment ids named in the error.

finding: §8.5.1 requires `cr post` without `--confirm` to 'print the full payload and exit 0 without posting'. §8.2.4 requires a suggestion failing validation to 'block posting with exit code 1 and name the record id', and §7.2.1 requires `cr post` to 'refuse to run when a marker is malformed' without naming any exit code. A dry run over a draft containing an invalid suggestion or a malformed marker therefore has two contradictory required exit codes, and one required behaviour has none — and §11.2's exit codes are pinned by a guard test.
suggestion: State that draft parsing and payload validation run before the confirmation gate and that their exit codes take precedence over §8.5.1, so a dry run over an invalid draft exits 1. Give §7.2.1 an explicit exit code (1).

finding: §9.1 lists eleven states and asserts in §9.1.2 that only `fixed` and `accepted` are terminal, but defines no transition graph and no command produces most of the states. `accepted` ("Reviewer waived it after discussion") has no command in §11 — `cr resolve` sets `fixed` only (§9.5.1), and there is no `cr accept`. §9.4 requires the agent to record exactly one of `fixed`, `partial`, or `regressed` for every `verifying` record, but §11 offers no command that records a verification outcome, and `cr record <pr> <file>` is specified in §6.5/§11 as recording a round's *merged findings*, never as transitioning existing records. `regressed` is non-terminal by §9.1.2 yet is omitted from §10.2.4's blocking list, so a PR can converge with a non-terminal record that has no defined exit.
suggestion: Add a transition table to §9.1 giving, for each state, the legal successors and the command that performs the transition. Add the missing command surface: either a `cr verify <id> --outcome fixed|partial|regressed` entry in §11 covering §9.4, or an explicit statement that `cr record` accepts state transitions for existing ids. Give `accepted` a producing command, and either make `regressed` terminal or add it to §10.2.4.

finding: 'Normalised' is load-bearing in at least four places and is defined in none: §9.2 'a normalised content hash of the anchored lines' (drives anchor migration and the stale-anchor state), §7.4.1 waiver key '(class, anchor content hash, normalised summary)', §2.6.3.1 harvest grouping 'by normalised body', and §3.3 claim text 'verbatim or minimally normalised'. Whether normalisation strips indentation, collapses internal whitespace, lowercases, or strips punctuation decides whether an anchor survives a reformat, whether a waiver still matches next round, and whether two comments group into a rule candidate. Two engineers produce incompatible hashes and mutually failing tests, and the QA checklist item 'the waiver survives the next round' has no expected value.
suggestion: Define one normalisation function in §1.1 (e.g. drop leading indentation, collapse runs of whitespace to a single space, strip trailing whitespace, preserve case) plus the hash algorithm and encoding, and reference it from §9.2, §7.4.1, §2.6.3.1 and §3.3. Replace 'verbatim or minimally normalised' in §3.3 with exactly one of the two.

finding: §5.5.3 forbids grading a finding with a probe from a different head, but no equivalent rule protects `cited` evidence. §9.2 migrates the finding's own anchor across a head change and §9.3 opens a new round, yet the path:line references stored in `evidence` (§6.1) are never re-resolved, re-hashed, or invalidated. A record raised in round 1 and posted in round 3 can therefore cite a line number that a force-push made meaningless, while still carrying the `cited` grade that licenses it to assert. Pointing a colleague at the wrong line is the cheapest and most visible way to be wrong.
suggestion: Extend §9.2 to re-resolve every cited path:line on every non-terminal record using the same content-hash-then-context procedure used for anchors, and mirror §5.5.3 with a clause stating that a citation which does not re-resolve at the current head demotes the record's grade — and therefore forces it to a question under §6.3. Report grade demotions in the round summary of §10.3.

finding: §9.4 requires the agent to record exactly one of `fixed`, `partial` or `regressed` for every `verifying` record, but no command in §11 accepts a verification outcome. `cr record <pr> <file>` is defined as `Record a round's merged findings`, `cr resolve` resolves a GitHub thread and sets `fixed` only after the outcome already exists, and `cr recheck` only moves records into `verifying`. There is also no way to express the linkage §9.4.3 requires between a regressed record and its original, since §6.1 has no such field.
suggestion: Add an explicit command to §11 (for example `cr verify <id> --outcome fixed|partial|regressed [--evidence <text>] [--regression <file>]`), or extend `cr record` to accept verification outcome records and say so. Add a `supersedes` or `regression_of` field to the §6.1 schema for the §9.4.3 link.

finding: §10.2.2 requires "every unit has a complete row of cells for every active role" without binding the cells to the current head. §9.3.5 opens a new round covering only the delta diff, so after a push the earlier units' cells are the ones written against a previous head. §2.3.3 requires every record to carry the head SHA it was produced against, and §5.5.3 uses that to forbid grading a finding from an off-head probe — but no equivalent rule exists for coverage cells, so convergence can be declared "proven" on coverage of code that has since changed. This is the one place the spec's own coverage-is-proven claim can be satisfied by stale evidence.
suggestion: Add to §4.5 or §10.2: a coverage cell is valid for the current head only when its unit's content hash is unchanged since the head the cell was produced against; a unit whose content changed MUST have its cells invalidated and re-filled, and §10.1 MUST report cells carried forward versus cells filled this round.

finding: §10.2.4 blocks convergence on records in `draft`, `queued`, `posted`, `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `verifying`, or `stale-anchor`. `regressed` is absent from the list even though §9.1.2 says 'Only `fixed` and `accepted` are terminal', so a PR with an open critical `regressed` record is reported as converged. `discarded` is in the same position: non-terminal by §9.1.2, absent from §10.2.4. A convergence test cannot decide what these two states do.
suggestion: Add `regressed` to the §10.2.4 list and name `discarded` as terminal in §9.1.2 alongside `fixed` and `accepted`; or rephrase §10.2.4 as 'no non-terminal record with severity critical or high' and make the §9.1 terminal set complete.

finding: §12.5 justifies --compact as omitting prose fields that an agent does not need to act, and lists `evidence`, `output_tail` and `input` among them. But §8.1.2 makes the agent the composer of every posted body, and the evidence, probe input and runner output are exactly what an honest body must restate to the author. Under --compact the agent writes the sentence a colleague will read from a summary with its support removed — which is the precise mechanism that produces prose that is plausible rather than true.
suggestion: Exclude the drafting and body-composition path from --compact: state that `cr draft` and any command emitting a prompt for reader-facing prose MUST include `evidence`, `probe` and `output_tail` regardless of the flag, and restrict --compact to list, status, and merge output.

finding: §2.3.3 requires that 'Every record MUST carry the head SHA it was produced against', but only the probe record (§5.5) has a `head` field. §6.1 carries `round` and no head, §3.3 claims carry none, and §3.4.5 enumerates a unit's required fields ('file paths, hunk ranges, and changed line count') without one. A test asserting §2.3.3 over `findings.ndjson`, `claims.ndjson`, or `units.ndjson` fails against the very schemas the spec defines.
suggestion: Add `head` to the §3.3, §3.4, §3.5 and §6.1 schemas, or narrow §2.3.3 to name the record types it governs and state that `round` is the head carrier for findings, with the round-to-head mapping stored in `meta.json`.

finding: `axes` in §2.4 is keyed 'per axis id', §2.5 requires a role to declare 'the axis this role serves', and §2.6 defaults a rule's `axis` to `convention`, but the set of valid axis ids is never enumerated. §4 gives prose headings, §4.5 refers to 'the test axis' and 'the intent axis', and §2.5.1 lists four role ids that may or may not be the axis ids. Since §2.5.3 and §2.6.5 abort with exit 3 on a malformed role, profile, or rule file, a validation test for the `axis` field cannot be written.
suggestion: Add a normative list of the four axis ids to §4 (e.g. `intent`, `correctness`, `convention`, `tests`) and require the `axis` field of roles and rules and the keys of `profile.axes` to be one of them, rejecting anything else with exit code 3.

finding: `axes` is defined in §2.4 as `Default enabled state per axis id`, §2.5 gives every role an `axis` field, §2.6 defaults a rule's `axis` to `convention`, and §4.5 turns axes on and off — but no section enumerates the legal axis ids. §4 names the four axes only as prose headings, and §2.5.1's ids (`intent-coverage`, `correctness`, `convention`, `test-adequacy`) are role ids, which §2.5 keeps deliberately separate from `axis`. Validation of profiles, roles and rules cannot be implemented without the enum.
suggestion: Add a sentence to §4 (or a row set to §2.4) fixing the axis ids as `intent`, `correctness`, `convention`, `tests` — or state explicitly that axis ids equal the four default role ids — and require profile, role and rule loaders to reject an unknown axis id with exit code 3.

finding: §2.4.1 makes profile selection automatic via `match.files` and §2.4.2 defines the no-match path, but nothing defines the multi-match path, and §2.4.3 makes the ambiguity certain by shipping `generic` alongside `laravel-pest`. If `generic` has empty `match.files` it never matches and §2.4.2 fires in every non-Laravel repository, making `generic` unreachable without an explicit per-repository override; if it matches everything, every Laravel repository matches two profiles with no stated precedence. Profiles are not merged anywhere in §2.4, so this is a choice of one, unspecified.
suggestion: Add a rule to §2.4: profiles are evaluated in a defined order (most specific `match.files` first, ties broken by id) and the first match wins; and state whether `generic` is a match-all profile or a fallback selected only when §2.4.2's no-match condition holds. Whichever it is, say it in §2.4.3 so the shipped corpus is unambiguous.

finding: §2.4.1 requires profile selection to be automatic 'via `match.files`', §2.4.2 specifies behaviour when 'no profile matches', and §2.4.3 requires shipping a `generic` profile. Nothing states what `generic.match.files` contains. If it matches everything, §2.4.2 is unreachable and its test is unwritable; if it matches nothing, `generic` never selects automatically and is reachable only through explicit configuration. §2.4.2 also requires disabling 'every axis that requires one' without saying which axes those are — §4.5 pins only the test axis.
suggestion: State explicitly whether `generic` is a catch-all or opt-in; if catch-all, replace §2.4.2 with the behaviour when only `generic` matches. Enumerate the axes that are disabled in the absence of a matching profile.

finding: §2.4.2 mandates behaviour when no profile matches, while §2.4.3 mandates shipping a `generic` profile. Whether `generic` carries universal `match.files` is never stated, so exactly one of the two is dead: if generic matches everything, §2.4.2's no-match branch is unreachable; if generic matches nothing, it is only ever reachable through an explicit `profile` override and the automatic selection of §2.4.1 never yields it. Profile selection also has no tie-break rule when two profiles' `match.files` both hit.
suggestion: State that `generic` is the declared fallback selected only when no other profile matches (and that §2.4.2's no-match branch applies to axes that generic cannot serve, such as tests when it declares no `tests.cmd`), or state that generic must be selected explicitly. Add a deterministic tie-break for multiple matches, such as most marker files matched, then lexical id order.

finding: §2.4.2 promises the honest path — no matching profile means report the situation and disable every axis that requires one — but §2.4.3 ships a `generic` profile and the spec never says how `generic` is selected, since `match.files` is meaningless for it. If it matches everything (the only way a generic profile is useful) then §2.4.2 becomes unreachable, and an unknown stack is reviewed under a profile with no real test command, no symbol language and no sandbox setup, while the output is indistinguishable from a properly profiled run. The dishonest path is the one that actually fires.
suggestion: Specify `generic` selection explicitly: it MUST be chosen only after every other profile fails to match, MUST be reported as a fallback by `cr brief` and `cr status` together with the axes it cannot serve, and MUST NOT satisfy §2.4.2's requirement to disable axes that need a real profile. A fallback profile must never be indistinguishable from a matched one in the output.

finding: §3.4.3 clusters hunks by enclosing symbol precisely so a unit is a coherent piece of work, and §3.4.4 then splits any cluster exceeding `cluster.max_lines` (default 80) changed lines, breaking exactly the grouping rule 3 established. The spec does not require a split unit to retain a reference to its siblings or to the symbol it came from, so a role reviewing fragment 2 of 3 judges code whose declarations and uses live in fragments it never sees. Reviewing a fragment out of context is one of the most reliable ways to produce a confident, wrong comment (this value is never used — it is, ninety lines later).
suggestion: Require every fragment produced by a split to record `parent_unit` and its sibling unit ids, require the prompt for a fragment to carry the full enclosing symbol as read-only context, and state that a finding whose supporting evidence lies outside its own fragment MUST be graded `argued` unless it cites the sibling unit explicitly.

finding: §3.5.3 suppresses a finding only when its anchor and class both match an existing human thread, and §6.4.1 dedups on the exact triple (anchor.path, anchor.line, class). A human reviewer's comment sits on whatever line they clicked, not on the line cr anchors to, and an ingested thread carries no kebab-case class at all — the spec never says how one is derived. The match will therefore almost never fire, and cr will restate what a colleague already said, in different words, two lines away. Repeating another reviewer costs standing with both the author and that reviewer.
suggestion: Widen thread suppression to a locality window rather than an exact line — the same file within the unit's hunk ranges, or the same enclosing symbol — and either specify how an ingested human thread acquires a class for comparison or drop class from the thread-matching key. When the match is near rather than exact, surface the existing thread inside the draft block so the human decides, instead of cr posting.

finding: A note is unverified hearsay — §3.6.3 admits sources chat and other — it is loaded automatically on every later round and every later PR resolving to the same key (§3.6.4), and §4.1.5 lets it suppress an unmapped-unit question outright. That is the mechanism by which cr's flagship check (VISION §2.1, the one it claims nobody else performs) is disabled permanently by one unverified sentence, on the agent's judgement that the note explains the unit. §11 offers `cr waivers remove` but no equivalent for notes: `cr note` writes and `cr context` prints, and nothing retracts, expires, or corrects.
suggestion: Add `cr note list` and `cr note remove <id>` to §11, require every note to carry an id, an actor, and the PR it was recorded from, and require §4.1.5 suppression to name the suppressing note id in the coverage cell and in the draft so the human sees which unmapped unit was excused by which unverified fact. Consider requiring notes past a configurable age to be re-affirmed rather than applied silently.

finding: §3.6.2 says `cr answer <question-id>` "MUST close the question", but "closed" is not one of §9.1's eleven states. The nearest state, `answered`, means something different ("Author replied without changing code"), is non-terminal by §9.1.2, and blocks convergence at critical or high severity per §10.2.4. A high-severity question that the author has answered to the reviewer's satisfaction therefore has no route to a terminal state, and §10.2 can never report the PR converged — which is the normal outcome for the question channel the whole design is built around.
suggestion: Add a terminal state such as `resolved-by-answer` to §9.1 and name `cr answer` as the command that produces it, or state that `cr answer` sets `accepted`. Either way, make §10.2.4's blocking list reference the terminal set from §9.1.2 rather than enumerating states independently, so the two cannot drift.

finding: §4.3.1 requires cr to search the repository for candidate pre-existing symbols for every function, method or class added by the diff, and §4.3.2 ranks by name similarity and signature shape with no minimum score and no cap on how many candidates are attached. Every trivially named helper therefore drags a list of weak matches into its unit's prompt, which the agent must read and dismiss — and §4.3.4 makes the resulting item a question in any case. That is agent tokens and wall-clock spent per unit with no corresponding reduction in the chance of a wrong assertion.
suggestion: Add `reinvention.min_similarity` and `reinvention.max_candidates` with conservative defaults, require cr to attach nothing when no candidate clears the threshold, and report the count of added symbols with no candidate so the axis is still honestly covered in §10.1.

finding: §4.4.1 requires every unit to be 'classified as covered, partially covered, or uncovered by tests changed or added in the PR', naming neither the actor nor the criterion. No profile field supplies coverage data — §2.4 has `tests.cmd`, `tests.filter_flag` and `tests.timeout_seconds` but no coverage command — so 'partially covered' has no observable basis and two testers will encode incompatible rules (a test file touching the same path, a test naming the symbol, line coverage above a threshold).
suggestion: State that the agent makes this classification and MUST record the reason in the cell, or add a coverage command to the profile and define the three classes as thresholds over the reported coverage of the unit's changed lines.

finding: §4.4.1 requires every unit to be `classified as covered, partially covered, or uncovered by tests changed or added in the PR`, and §4.4.2 requires expected edge cases to be enumerated per claim, with neither naming an actor. §4.3.1 by contrast says explicitly `cr MUST search`, which establishes that the section does attribute work when it means cr. No coverage tooling exists in the §2.4 profile schema, and deciding which test exercises which unit is a semantic judgement, so cr cannot do it — but the spec never says the agent must.
suggestion: Prefix each requirement in §4.1, §4.2 and §4.4 with its actor, as §4.3.1 does, and state that cr's contribution to §4.4.1 is limited to listing the test files touched by the diff in the unit brief while the classification itself is a role output recorded in the coverage cell.

finding: §4.4.2 requires that for every claim the expected edge cases be enumerated and each marked asserted, missing, or not applicable with a reason. Expected edge cases is an open set defined by nobody, so the enumeration is unbounded, unfalsifiable, and impossible to audit for completeness — while §4.4.4 forces every resulting finding without a probe to a question and §5.6.4 caps probes at 10 per round, so most of the enumeration cannot be converted into evidence at all. The cost scales with claims times the agent's imagination and buys questions.
suggestion: Bound the enumeration to a countable set cr can present: edge cases derived from the claim text and from the changed branches of the unit, capped per claim by a configurable limit. Alternatively require enumeration only for claims whose units §4.4.1 classified as uncovered or partially covered, and require the not-applicable reason only where a case was actually considered.

finding: §5.2.1 records 'a truncated tail of output' and §5.5 defines `output_tail` as 'Truncated runner output'. No limit in bytes or lines is given, no configuration key exists for it, it is not stated whether stdout and stderr are interleaved or separate, and no marker indicates that truncation occurred. A truncation test has no expected value, and §12.5's `--compact` omission of `output_tail` cannot be checked against a known baseline.
suggestion: Add a `tests.output_tail_lines` (or bytes) profile or config setting with a stated default, say whether stdout and stderr are merged, and require a marker line when output was truncated so the test can assert the boundary.

finding: §5.3.3 guarantees that a mutation is reverted "even when the run fails or times out", but §5.4.2's gap probe — which places a new test file into the sandbox, runs it, and removes it — carries no equivalent guarantee. A gap probe that times out per §5.2.3 or errors therefore leaves an orphan test file in the sandbox, which the next `cr test` baseline run (§5.2.2) will execute, corrupting the baseline that §5.3's disproof logic depends on. The asymmetry is in the spec text, not merely an implementation risk.
suggestion: Add to §5.4: the test file MUST be removed even when the run fails, errors, or times out, mirroring §5.3.3. Consider hoisting the guarantee to §5.6 as a single statement covering every probe kind, so a future probe kind inherits it.

finding: §5.4.3 asserts that a failing gap probe means the behaviour is wrong and mandates severity at least high. The test is written by the agent (§5.4.1), so a failing probe equally means the agent misread the intended behaviour and encoded its misreading as an experiment — and the spec converts that directly into a high-severity claim with a reproduction attached. Nothing requires the probe's premise (what behaviour it asserts, and which claim licenses that expectation) to travel with the comment, and §12.5 lets --compact strip the probe `input` entirely.
suggestion: Weaken the wording to: a failing gap probe shows the behaviour differs from the probe's expectation. Require the record to cite the claim id that justifies the expectation, and force it to a question regardless of grade when no claim justifies it. Require the probe `input` to be quoted in the drafted body so the author can check the premise rather than only the failure output.

finding: §5.5 presents a single flat enum `no-test-failed | failed | passed | error | timeout`, but §5.3.4-5 use `no-test-failed`/`failed` for mutations while §5.4.3-4 speak of failing and passing gap probes. A green suite is `no-test-failed` for a mutation and `passed` for a gap probe — the same mechanical observation recorded under two different names — and the table never says the mapping is kind-dependent. No requirement anywhere states when `error` is recorded, so that value has no test.
suggestion: Either make the enum purely mechanical and kind-independent (`passed`, `failed`, `error`, `timeout`) and let §5.3/§5.4 supply the interpretation, or annotate each table value with the probe kind it applies to. Add a requirement defining `error` (e.g. the patch did not apply, or the runner could not start).

finding: §5.6.1 names the probe/test lock after the profile id, with the rationale "so two `cr` runs never share a test database". A test database is a property of a repository (or a checkout), not of a profile: two unrelated repositories that both resolve to `laravel-pest`, or every repository that falls back to `generic`, will serialise against each other for no reason, each waiting the full `probe.lock_timeout_seconds` (300) before failing with exit code 4 per §5.6.2. Conversely the key is not narrow enough to be safe either, since §5.1 places the sandbox per PR while nothing states whether two PRs in the same repository may run probes concurrently.
suggestion: Key the lock on `(owner, repo, profile id)` at minimum, and state explicitly whether concurrent probe runs on two PRs of the same repository are permitted. If the underlying resource is genuinely a shared test database, add a profile field naming the lock resource so a profile can widen or narrow it.

finding: §6.2.1 says the grade `MUST be computed by cr from the record, never asserted by the agent`, but §6.1 lists `grade` as a record field and §6.2.2 speaks of `A record claiming probed`. So the agent both does and does not supply the field. Only the `probed` mismatch has a defined outcome (exit 1); a record arriving as `cited` that computes to `argued`, or vice versa, has no specified behaviour — reject, overwrite silently, or overwrite and report.
suggestion: State that `grade` is output-only: `cr` ignores any agent-supplied value except that a supplied `probed` without a valid same-head probe is rejected with exit 1, and every other supplied value is overwritten by the computed grade and the overwrite is counted in the round summary. Mark `grade` in the §6.1 table as computed.

finding: §6.4.2 breaks duplicate-group ties by 'the earliest role in corpus order'. Corpus order is never defined: it could be the resolution layering of §2.5.4 (per-repository, then global, then built-in), lexical file order, or the order roles are listed in `meta.json`. The representative of a duplicate group — which decides the posted text and the reported overlap — is therefore not reproducible, contradicting §2.1.1.
suggestion: Define corpus order explicitly, e.g. 'the order in which active roles are listed in `meta.json`, which is the §2.5.4 resolution order with remaining ties broken lexically by role id', and state it once in §2.5.

finding: §6.5.1 requires `cr merge <files...> -o <out>` to apply §6.4, which needs repository-scoped waivers (§7.4.1), `the earliest role in corpus order` (§6.4.2) and a round to count waiver drops against (§7.4.2). The signature carries no PR or repository argument, so none of those are resolvable. §5.3.2 and §5.4.2 show the same drift in the other direction, spelling `cr probe run --kind mutation ...` without the `<pr>` that §11 requires.
suggestion: Give merge a PR argument (`cr merge <pr> <files...> -o <out>`) or state that it resolves the repository from `--repo` plus the working directory and defers waiver filtering to `cr record`. Make the §5.3.2 and §5.4.2 invocations match the §11 signature exactly.

finding: §6.5.2 requires `cr merge` to fail with exit code 1 on "missing required fields" and name the offending line, but no section says which of §6.1's eighteen fields are required. Only `suggestion` is marked optional, in prose; `rule`, `claim`, `probe`, and `thread_id` are all conditional by their own definitions, and `id`, `state`, `round`, and `grade` are arguably cr's to assign rather than the agent's to supply. The validation is not implementable, and the same ambiguity governs what an agent must emit into a per-role NDJSON file.
suggestion: Add a `Required` column to the §6.1 table with values `agent`, `cr`, or `conditional`, and state in §6.5 that only fields marked `agent` are validated at merge time. At minimum, name the agent-supplied required set explicitly in §6.5.2.

finding: §7.1.5 requires regeneration to 'preserve existing bodies for records the user already edited', but nothing in §2.3 or §7.1 stores the body as originally rendered, so `cr` has no observable way to distinguish an edited body from an unedited one. The rule is also silent about records that have since been waived or discarded, and about user-added `id=new` blocks, which have no record to regenerate from.
suggestion: Require `cr` to store the rendered body (or its hash) per record when the draft is written, define 'edited' as 'the current body differs from the stored rendering', and state what regeneration does with `id=new` blocks and with records no longer in `queued`.

finding: §7.2 states that triage happens by editing the file and that `cr post` interprets the result, so deleting a block only becomes a discard and a waiver at post time. But §7.1.5 requires the draft to be regenerable and specifies preservation only for "existing bodies for records the user already edited" — a deleted block has no body to preserve and no waiver yet exists, so regenerating the draft before posting resurrects every discarded record. §9.3.5 opening a new round for a delta hits the same path.
suggestion: Either make deletion durable at draft-regeneration time by requiring `cr draft` to diff the on-disk draft against the previous render and record deletions as discards before re-rendering, or specify that `cr draft` MUST refuse to overwrite a draft that has been edited since it was written unless `--force` is given, and say which records a forced regeneration drops.

finding: The `id=new` row of §7.2 admits arbitrary user-authored comments into the posted review, but nothing specifies how such a block is handled. It has no §6.1 record — so no `class` (which §7.3.1 requires for every triage event, and §6.4.1 for dedup), no `axis`, no `role`, no `grade`, and no `unit`. It is unclear whether it is anchored and anchor-validated per §6.1.2, whether §8.2 suggestion validation applies to a suggestion inside it, whether it enters `findings.ndjson` and therefore §9's re-review lifecycle, and what id it receives given §6.1's `f<n>` scheme.
suggestion: Specify in §7.2 that a manual block is materialised as a full §6.1 record on post, with `grade` omitted or a new value such as `authored`, `role: human`, a required `class` in the marker, an anchor validated exactly like any other, and a freshly allocated `f<n>` id — and state explicitly whether it participates in §9 re-review and §7.3 statistics.

finding: The deletion row of §7.2 collapses two different reviewer intents into one irreversible action: this is wrong, and this is true but not worth saying here. Both write a waiver that §7.4.1 scopes to the repository rather than the PR, so a correct finding deleted once as too minor is silenced everywhere forever. Both are also counted identically by §7.3.1, so not-now deletions push a precise class toward demotion under §7.3.3 on evidence that says nothing about its precision — the statistics that are supposed to measure correctness end up measuring appetite.
suggestion: Distinguish the verbs at the marker level: deleting a block means wrong, waive repository-wide, while a `disposition=skip` marker attribute (or a blanked body) means correct but not this round — dropped from this draft, no waiver written, and excluded from the demotion statistics. Require §7.3.2 to report the two counts separately.

finding: §7.1.1 puts `id`, `kind`, `path`, `line`, `severity`, and `grade` into an editable marker, but §7.2 defines the effect of editing only `kind` finding→question (soften) and `path`/`line` (re-validate). The spec is silent on editing `kind` question→finding, `severity`, `grade`, and `id`. The question→finding direction is the exact route around §6.3.1's forcing: a record cr computed as `argued` and forced to a question can be promoted back to an assertion by editing one word in a Markdown file, with no confirmation, no record, and no appearance in the §6.3.2 forcing count. An editable `grade` field is worse, since §6.2.1 says the grade is cr's to compute and never asserted.
suggestion: Declare the marker fields read-only except `kind` (soften only) and `path`/`line`. Specify that `cr post` MUST reject an edit that promotes `kind=question` to `kind=finding` on a record whose computed grade is `argued`, MUST reject any edit to `grade`, `id`, or `severity`, and MUST name the record id and line when it does.

finding: §7.2 lets the user add a block with `id=new`, posted as a manual comment. §6.1 requires every record to carry `kind`, `axis`, `role`, `class`, `severity`, `grade`, `unit` and an anchor, and a user-authored block supplies none of them. Dedup keys on `class` (§6.4.1), triage statistics key on class, axis, role and grade (§7.3.1), a deletion of such a block would need a waiver key that includes a normalised summary (§7.4.1), and §8.2 suggestion validation still applies. Nothing states what id such a block is assigned once posted, or how it appears in coverage and the round summary.
suggestion: Define the manual-comment record explicitly: assign the next `f<n>` id at post time, set `role` and `axis` to a reserved `manual` value, `grade` to `cited` or exempt it from grading, require only `path` and `line` in the marker, and exclude manual records from triage statistics and demotion analysis so they cannot skew §7.3.3.

finding: §7.3.3 demotes a class whose 'discard-plus-soften rate exceeds `stats.demote_threshold` (default 0.6) over at least `stats.min_samples` (default 8) events'. The denominator is unstated — `raised` from §7.3.2, or `kept + softened + discarded` — and they differ, because a raised record may have been deduplicated or waived and never triaged at all. 'Event' is undefined, and no window is given (all history, or a trailing window like `rules.dead_after` in §2.6.3.4). Two testers computing the same triage log will disagree on whether a class is a demotion candidate.
suggestion: Define the rate as (softened + discarded) / (kept + softened + discarded), counting only triage events; define an event as one triage decision on one record in one round; and state the window over which events are counted.

finding: §7.3.3 lists a class over `stats.demote_threshold` as a demotion candidate with the recommendation to default it to question. The recommendation has no addressee and no mechanism: nothing in §6 or §7 consumes it. A class the human has discarded or softened in more than 60% of at least 8 observed events keeps asserting at colleagues, round after round, until somebody hand-edits a role or rule file. The feedback loop the trust economy depends on terminates in a printed report, so the empirical evidence that a class is wrong never changes what gets posted.
suggestion: Make demotion automatic and reversible: once a class crosses the threshold cr forces its records to kind: question at record time (the §6.3 machinery already exists), reports the demotion in the round summary of §10.3, and requires an explicit `cr stats promote <class> --confirm` with a recorded reason to restore assertion.

finding: §7.4.1 keys a waiver on a "normalised summary" and §2.6.3.1 groups harvest candidates by "normalised body", but neither normalisation is defined anywhere. These are not cosmetic: the waiver key determines whether a false positive the human already deleted comes back, and §2.1.1 requires every command to be reproducible given the same inputs. Two implementations, or the same implementation across two versions, will produce different waiver keys and silently resurrect waived findings. §9.2's "normalised content hash of the anchored lines" has the same problem for the other component of the key.
suggestion: Define each normalisation concretely in the section that uses it — for the summary and comment body, at least case folding, whitespace collapse, and stripping of code spans and `path:line` tokens; for anchored lines, leading-whitespace and trailing-whitespace handling and whether comments are stripped. Add a statement that changing a normalisation is a breaking change requiring waiver-key migration, since §7.4.1 scopes waivers to the repository and they outlive any one PR.

finding: §8.1.4: 'A question body SHOULD end with an explicit question, and `cr` MUST warn when a `kind=question` body contains none.' The SHOULD constrains the ending while the MUST tests for containment, so a body with a question in the middle passes the check and violates the guidance. 'Explicit question' is never defined, and bodies are rendered in the configured language (`render.lang`, default `tr`), so the only implementable reading — presence of a `?` character — is not the one written.
suggestion: Collapse to one observable rule: '`cr` MUST warn when a `kind=question` body contains no `?` character', and either drop the SHOULD or align it with the check.

finding: §8.2.3: 'Leading whitespace of the first replaced line MUST be preserved unless the suggestion explicitly changes indentation.' A validator cannot observe intent, so the exception makes the rule either vacuous (any differing indentation is by definition an explicit change) or a blanket rejection of every re-indentation suggestion. §8.2.4 makes a validation failure block posting with exit code 1, so a pinned exit code hangs on an undecidable predicate; two testers will write opposite expectations for the same suggestion.
suggestion: Replace the intent clause with something observable: either 'the suggestion is taken as-is and `cr` MUST warn when the first suggestion line's leading whitespace differs from the first replaced line', or add an explicit per-record flag (e.g. `reindent: true`) that disables the check.

finding: §8.3.1 posts every comment of a round as one GitHub review and §8.4.1 says that if the review call fails no state MUST be marked posted. Neither clause covers the ambiguous case — a timeout or dropped connection after GitHub has accepted the review — so the documented recovery is to retry, which posts the entire review a second time. Duplicating a whole review on a colleague's PR is the loudest available way to spend credibility, and the spec already has the data to prevent it, since §8.3.3 writes rounds/<n>/posted.json before the network call.
suggestion: Require reconciliation before retry: on any non-clean failure mark the round post-unknown and exit 4, and require the next `cr post` to fetch the PR's existing reviews and match them against rounds/<n>/posted.json before it may send anything. Embed a round-and-head fingerprint in a leading hidden marker of the review body so an already-posted round is detectable without heuristics.

finding: §8.5.1 says `cr post` without `--confirm` MUST print the full payload and `exit 0 without posting`. §8.2.4 says a suggestion failing validation MUST block posting with exit code 1, and §7.2.1 says post MUST refuse to run on a malformed marker. A dry run over a draft with an invalid suggestion is therefore required to exit both 0 and 1, and the relative order of gate and validation is never stated.
suggestion: Specify that validation always runs before the gate, and that §8.5.1's exit 0 applies only when validation passes; a dry run over invalid input exits 1 (validation) or 2 as appropriate and posts nothing. Add a sentence to §8.5.1 to that effect.

finding: §6.1 defines `state` as `State per §9.1`, but two mandated outcomes have no state in that table: §3.5.3 requires a suppressed finding to be `recorded as suppressed_by_thread`, and §6.4.3 requires suppressed duplicates to be retained with a pointer to the representative. Neither can be stored in a `state` restricted to the eleven listed values.
suggestion: Add `suppressed-by-thread` and `suppressed-duplicate` to the §9.1 table with their meanings, mark both non-terminal but excluded from the §10.2 convergence blockers, and add the `duplicate_of` and `suppressed_by` pointer fields to the §6.1 schema.

finding: Three distinct normalisations are required and none is defined: the anchor's `normalised content hash` (§9.2), the `normalised summary` in the waiver key (§7.4.1), and the `normalised body` used to group comments for rule harvesting (§2.6.3.1).
